measures_publication_dispatch.dispatch_body:
﻿The Hole in the Map
Mapped & Measured | unDrifted


AI data centers are usually introduced as technology infrastructure, but that description becomes inadequate almost as soon as the conversation moves beyond the servers.


At Nashville’s September 16 Innovators Forum: AI Data Centers, the discussion moved across power, water, land, design, public health, financing, regulation, community impact, and long-term operations. The forum was co-hosted by Julia Polk of Curio and Dr. Reed Omary, with Ross Hamilton of Gensler and Metro Nashville Council Member At-Large Burkley Allen among the featured guests. The event itself was framed around the impact of AI data-center development and Nashville’s newly adopted regulatory response.


What emerged was less a debate about a single kind of building than a picture of the many environments required to make that building possible.


MAPPED


What the forum put on the map


Electrical demand was one of the clearest parts of that picture. A large data center does not simply connect to the grid like another office building. Its presence can require generation capacity, substations, transformers, transmission infrastructure, backup systems, and long-term utility planning. Once those requirements are considered together, the data center stops looking like an isolated technology project and starts looking like a new participant in the regional energy system.


Water enters the picture through cooling. Different cooling architectures can place very different demands on local water systems, which means a design choice inside the facility can change the relationship between the project and the environment outside it. Water availability, sewer capacity, climate, cooling technology, and future operating changes all matter. Cooling is therefore not merely an engineering detail; it is part of the facility’s continuing relationship with the place supporting it.


Land and siting add another layer. The site itself may have to accommodate not only the principal building but also mechanical equipment, substations, generators, security infrastructure, utility corridors, stormwater systems, lighting, setbacks, and access requirements. Metro’s own legislative record recognizes that modern data centers can have land-use effects materially different from ordinary office, warehouse, telecommunications, utility, or industrial uses, including noise, vibration, lighting, stormwater impacts, fuel storage, battery systems, emergency-response concerns, and continuous twenty-four-hour operation.


The built environment therefore extends well beyond the walls containing the computers. Ross Hamilton’s design perspective was useful in that context because it kept the physical facility connected to everything required to support it: roads, utilities, equipment yards, cooling systems, power infrastructure, and the surrounding uses that already occupy the area.


Health and sustainability entered through many of those same systems. Energy, water, noise, heat, air quality, emergency preparedness, and infrastructure decisions ultimately become conditions experienced by people. Dr. Omary’s presence brought that relationship into the room without requiring the conversation to treat health as a separate subject. The health environment is affected by choices made in the energy, water, design, and operating environments.


Finance also belongs on the map. Data-center development can involve private capital, utility investment, incentives, infrastructure spending, and long-term assumptions about demand. Those financial structures determine more than who pays for construction. They shape who absorbs risk, who benefits from growth, and how much of the supporting infrastructure remains useful to the surrounding community.


Public systems are part of the environment as well. Planning departments, utilities, zoning authorities, emergency responders, elected officials, and regulatory agencies all contribute time and capacity to making a project possible and monitoring it afterward. Their work is rarely represented as a resource flowing into the development, but it is one nonetheless.


The community sits inside all of these environments at once. Residents may encounter the project through their electric system, water system, neighborhood, tax structure, roads, public meetings, employment opportunities, or changes to nearby land. That makes meaningful participation difficult when the information needed to understand the project is scattered across technical studies, utility decisions, zoning records, financial agreements, and public hearings.


The forum’s value was that those subjects were not treated as unrelated side effects. Taken together, they formed a map of the environment required to support AI infrastructure.


The environments involved


The visual brings those relationships into one frame: energy, water, land, built environment, public systems, community, health, and the economic environment. Beside them, the resource ledger shows another feature of the system. Many of the inputs can be quantified with increasing precision, while the value returning to the surrounding community is usually recorded in separate places, under different rules, or not expressed as a single public measure at all.


The illustrative figures in the ledger represent a 100 MW U.S. data-center example. They are not measurements of a particular Nashville project.


![The environments involved and resource ledger — illustrative 100 MW data-center scale](https://zfihrspxvennjzazxcbj.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/prism/mm_%20desk_resource_ledger_hole_in_the_map.webp)

MEASURED


The map exposes an imbalance that is easy to miss when each resource is considered separately.


A large data center can express its electrical requirement in megawatts. Water demand can be estimated in gallons. Land can be measured in acres. Substations and transmission infrastructure can be identified. Incentives can be documented. Planning and permitting requirements can be traced through public records. The inputs leave evidence because each supporting system has some reason to count what it provides.


The return is harder to read as one relationship.


Employment figures may appear in one place, tax revenue in another, and incentives somewhere else. Infrastructure improvements may primarily serve the project while also producing public benefit. Local procurement can be distributed across contractors and vendors. Community investments may result from negotiated commitments, voluntary programs, or individual partnerships. Educational and research benefits may be real without ever being assembled into a public account of what remained locally.


That does not mean nothing comes back. It means the return is fragmented.


The hole in the map


The data center itself is extensively mapped. Its parcel, power requirement, utility connections, permits, equipment, and operating conditions all generate records. The surrounding environments are also measured, but largely within their own administrative boundaries.


Power remains a utility matter. Water remains a utility matter. Land use remains a planning matter. Incentives and financing live in their own agreements. Emergency response sits inside another institution. Community effects surface through hearings, testimony, studies, complaints, employment data, and public commitments.


Each record can be accurate and still leave the overall exchange difficult to see.


That is the hole in the map: not the facility itself, but the missing relationship between what the surrounding environments provide and what remains visible in return.


What Nashville is already measuring


Nashville’s current framework begins to address part of this problem by treating data centers as a distinct land use rather than assuming that older classifications adequately describe them.


Metro ordinance BL2026-1391, which became effective July 31, established five data-center use types and created new application and continuing-compliance requirements. Developers covered by the framework may need written confirmation of electricity and water/sewer capacity, along with a noise-impact assessment, water-consumption and sustainability plan, energy-consumption and sustainability plan, lighting plan, transmission-line impact assessment, and other information requested by reviewing agencies.


The ordinance also requires operators to submit an annual compliance report describing changes to the assessments submitted during the zoning process and demonstrating continued compliance with applicable requirements and conditions.


That requirement matters because the facility operating five years from now may not be the same facility described at approval. Compute loads can increase, cooling systems can change, ownership can change, buildings can expand, and supporting utility infrastructure can evolve. Annual reporting gives Metro a mechanism for seeing some of that movement instead of treating approval as the final observation point.


Earlier in the same regulatory process, Metro also adopted a temporary moratorium on certain data-center permitting while the new framework was being considered. The moratorium legislation specifically cited concerns ranging from high electrical demand and cooling systems to noise, stormwater, security, and emergency response.


Nashville has therefore already recognized that the operating conditions around a data center matter beyond the initial construction decision.


The next useful measure: material change


Continuing compliance and environmental change are related, but they are not identical.


A facility can remain within established requirements while the relationship between the project and the surrounding environment changes substantially. A larger electrical load, different cooling technology, expansion onto additional land, a new substation, changed ownership, or a revised community commitment can alter that relationship even when each individual change is permitted.


That makes material change a useful editorial concept for understanding what comes after compliance reporting. The point is not to treat every modification as a problem. It is to recognize when enough has changed that the original map no longer describes the operating environment particularly well.


Compliance asks whether the established conditions are being followed. A deeper environmental review would ask whether those conditions still describe the system that now exists.


The resource ledger


The resource ledger gives that relationship a practical form.


At an illustrative 100 MW scale, continuous electrical demand would equal approximately 876 GWh per year if the facility operated at that full load continuously. Water use varies widely by cooling system, climate, facility design, and power source, so the ledger treats national estimates as examples rather than Nashville-specific facts. Land requirements vary just as widely, ranging from relatively dense facilities to campuses occupying tens or even hundreds of acres once supporting infrastructure is included.


Those measurable inputs sit alongside less easily standardized demands such as transmission upgrades, substations, roads, materials, financing, public planning capacity, regulatory attention, and emergency-response capability.


The return side has no comparable standard ledger. Jobs are project-specific. Tax contribution depends on ownership, incentives, and tax structure. Local procurement depends on contracting decisions. Infrastructure improvements may produce public value, private value, or both. Community investment and educational partnerships depend on individual agreements.


That asymmetry is itself worth measuring. The resources entering the environment are increasingly legible, while the value returning to the surrounding community remains distributed across different systems.


A more complete public account would not need to prescribe one identical return for every project. It would simply make the relationship easier to see: what the environment supplied, what changed because the project arrived, what persisted locally, and whether those conditions continued to hold over time.


What Nashville has begun


The forum did not produce a single answer for Nashville, and it would be misleading to write as though it did. What it did was make the system visible.


Nashville has already begun measuring more of the operating environment around data centers through its zoning and reporting requirements. The next challenge is not merely collecting more numbers. It is making the relationship among those numbers understandable enough that the public can see the whole exchange rather than a series of disconnected records.


The hole in the map is where those records stop connecting.


About this report


This Mapped & Measured article draws from the September 16, 2026 Innovators Forum: AI Data Centers during 3686 week in Nashville, Metro Nashville’s public legislative record, and live AI-assisted notes from the discussion.


The Mapped section summarizes themes surfaced during the forum and does not attribute specific statements to individual panelists unless independently documented. The Measured section is unDrifted editorial analysis of the environmental relationships and measurement gaps made visible by that discussion.


Illustrative resource figures in the accompanying ledger describe a 100 MW U.S. data-center example and should not be read as measurements of a specific Nashville facility.


unDrifted is the editorial and research publication of Measures Registry.
